topic: Money: its history (barter to electronic money) and making good choices with money.

readingSkill.name: Identifying problems and solutions
readingSkill.bookDefinition: A problem is something difficult that happens in stories and in our lives. We can fix problems. A solution is a way to fix the problem.

pageMap.section: Unit opener: Activating Prior Knowledge About Money
pageMap.contains: Title 'How Much Is It?'. Photo of two money jars labelled 'Donating: Save the Animals' and 'Saving: Gift for Mom'.

A-C: what labels do you want on your jars; model 'Do you want a label for college?' / 'Of course I do!' / 'We both want labels for college.' D: Where do people use money? class list. E: picture of two farmers: 'One farmer needs a goat. The other farmer needs some grain.' What's wrong? How can they fix it? Banner: Now read The History of Money.
Barter, around 6000 BCE (goat paid with grain); 1200 BCE cowrie shells. Callout explaining BCE: 'BCE stands for Before Common Era.' + 'Can you guess what CE stands for?'

1000 BCE China: metal knives and spades; 400-300 BCE round metal money with holes; 600 BCE Lydia (part of modern-day Turkey): first true coins with pictures of plants and animals. Question: 'Why do you think they put holes in the coins?' Words in Context: bartered, metal, valuable, credit card, plastic.

Countries made coins from valuable metals like silver and gold; first paper money from China 800-900 CE; Europe around 1600 CE. Note: 'A timeline is an infographic that shows information in time order.' Timeline: 1200 BCE cowrie shells, 1000 BCE knives and spades, 600 BCE first coins.

1958 first credit card (small plastic card); 21st century electronic money, used to buy things on the internet. Questions: 'What type of money do you think is going to be next?' and 'Do you wish we used different money today?' Timeline: 800-900 CE first paper money, 1958 CE first credit card.
A: Which of these is or was money? (6 pictures). B: chart Type of Money / When It Was Used / What It Was Made From. C: Design the next type of money: 'I think the next type of money will be ...'

objectives.source: added (the book does not print objectives; written from the page content)
unit: Pupils will be able to name 5 kinds of money from the reading (cowrie shells, metal knives and spades, coins, paper money, credit cards) and put them in time order.
Pupils will be able to find a problem and a solution in a story and in an informational text.
Pupils will be able to retell The $100 Bill in 5 simple sentences using the past tense (found, put, went, said, smiled).
Pupils will be able to say what they would do with found money using 'I would ...' and 'I should ...'.
Pupils will be able to ask and answer about prices: 'How much is it?' 'It's ... dollars.'
Pupils will be able to read and spell words with the ar pattern (park, hard, card, car).
canDo: I can say how people paid for things long ago.
I can find the problem and the solution in a story.
I can say what Paige did with the $100.
I can say what I would do with money I find.
I can ask 'How much is it?' and answer.
I can read and write words with ar.
successCriteria: Orders 4 timeline cards correctly (shells 1200 BCE, knives and spades 1000 BCE, first coins 600 BCE, paper money 800-900 CE, credit card 1958).
Completes 'Problem: ... Solution: ...' for the story with one sentence each.
Says at least 3 true past-tense sentences about Paige.
Gives an opinion with a reason: 'I would ... because ...'.

readings.title: The History of Money
summaryAdded: Long ago people did not use money. They bartered (traded things).
Later people used cowrie shells because shells were easy to carry.
In China people used metal knives and spades, then round metal money with holes.
In Lydia (part of modern-day Turkey) a king made the first true coins.
China made the first paper money. In 1958 there was the first credit card.
Today many people use electronic money to buy things on the internet.

timeline.money: round metal money with holes in the middle (China)
first paper money (China); Europe around 1600 CE

keyLinesBook.text: Thousands of years ago, people didn't use money.
The shells were easier to carry than goats or bags of grain.
But this money was difficult to carry and to use.
This made buying and selling easier.

problemsAndSolutions.problem: Barter: it took time to agree how much things were worth; goats and grain are heavy.
Metal knives and spades were difficult to carry and to use.
problemsAndSolutions.solution: Round metal money with holes, then coins.
Paper money (easier to carry than metal coins).

sequenceAdded: After school, Jodie and Nina laugh because Paige doesn't have a cell phone.
Paige walks home through the park and sees something in the leaves.
She finds a wet, dirty $100 bill. There is no way to return it.
Jodie comes. Paige puts the money in her pocket.
Paige looks at a $95 phone in a store, but she doesn't buy it.
At home Dad is tired. Money is tight.
Paige pays, and she and Dad go to a restaurant.
